concept.name: Commodity future
concept.definition: A futures contract on a physical commodity: a standardized, exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a specified quantity and grade of an agricultural product, metal, or energy product at a price set at initiation, for delivery or cash settlement in a specified future month.
concept.intuition: A commodity future locks in today the price of wheat, oil, or gold for a future month, letting producers and users shift price risk to those willing to bear it.
concept.mechanics: Contracts specify quantity, grade, delivery points, and delivery month, are margined with daily settlement, and most positions are offset before delivery rather than delivered. Futures prices reflect the spot price plus the cost of carry (storage, insurance, financing), producing contango (rising curve) or backwardation (falling curve) term structures.
concept.formula: Carrying-charge approximation: F approximately S x (1 + cost of carry), where S is the spot price and the cost of carry includes storage, insurance, and interest.
concept.failure_modes: Delivery squeezes and corners can dislocate prices, and storage or transport constraints can even drive prices negative (WTI, April 2020). Hedgers face basis risk between their local cash market and the contract's delivery grade and location, and volatile markets trigger heavy margin calls.
concept.misconceptions: That futures traders usually take or make delivery — the vast majority of positions are offset before expiry. Also, the futures price is not a pure forecast of the future spot price; it embeds carrying costs and risk premia.
concept.example: A wheat farmer sells December wheat futures at $6.50 per bushel to lock in a harvest-time price; if harvest cash prices fall to $6.00, the futures gain offsets the lower crop revenue.
